fact: Blood Falls runs clear when it emerges from beneath hundreds of metres of Antarctic ice. It turns blood-red only after its iron-rich, hypersaline brine hits air, oxidises and forms amorphous iron nanospheres.
locationContext: Taylor Valley · McMurdo Dry Valleys, East Antarctica

fact: Socotra is so biologically isolated that about 95% of its land-snail species and 90% of its reptile species occur nowhere else on Earth.
Rocks weighing as much as 320 kilograms can travel across Death Valley’s Racetrack Playa. Thin floating ice, shallow water and winds of only about 10 mph can move them in near-perfect synchrony.
Lençóis Maranhenses looks like a vast desert, yet rainwater alone creates thousands of clear seasonal lagoons between its white dunes, while some dunes migrate up to 25 metres in a year.
The 40-kilometre-wide Eye of the Sahara looks so much like an impact crater that scientists once classified it as one. It is actually the eroded remains of a colossal uplifted geologic dome.
locationContext: Adrar Plateau · central Mauritania, north-west Africa

fact: Mono Lake is roughly twice as salty as the ocean, and one of its islands contains lake-bottom mud that magma physically pushed above the water only a few centuries ago.
Lake Turkana is the world’s largest permanent desert lake, and fossils from its shores have contributed more to our understanding of human ancestry than those from any other place on Earth.
One lake holds about 20% of all the unfrozen freshwater on Earth. Lake Baikal is also the planet’s deepest lake and is estimated to be 25 million years old.

Lake Natron is too caustic for most familiar life, but its salt-loving microorganisms turn it red. Receding water also leaves moat-like channels that protect vast flamingo nesting grounds from predators.
locationContext: Arusha Region · northern Tanzania, East Africa

fact: When a thin layer of rainwater covers Salar de Uyuni, the world’s largest salt flat becomes a mirror spanning thousands of square kilometres, erasing the visual boundary between ground and sky.

Tsingy de Bemaraha is a forest made of razor-edged limestone needles. Its canyons and pinnacles isolate pockets of woodland so effectively that rare species evolved in tiny natural islands within the stone maze.

On Jeju Island, women divers, some in their 80s, descend about 10 metres without oxygen tanks and can work for up to seven hours a day. They hold their breath for every dive and make a unique sound when they surface.
locationContext: Jeju Province · South Korea, East Asia

source: ThisisFINLAND · Ministry for Foreign Affairs of Finland
fact: Finland has been counted at 53.2 heavy-metal bands per 100,000 people, more per person than any other country. Tiny Lemi once entered 13 bands among only 3,076 residents and was crowned World Capital of Metal.

place: The world's most linguistically diverse country
fact: Papua New Guinea holds the record for the most living languages in one country: 840 were documented in 2019. Most of those languages are spoken by fewer than 1,000 people.
locationContext: Papua New Guinea · south-west Pacific, Oceania

fact: In the Voladores ceremony, four men launch themselves from a pole up to 40 metres high and spiral towards the ground on ropes. A fifth remains balanced on top, playing a flute and drum to honour the sun, winds and cardinal directions.
In Vanuatu, one finger turns sand, volcanic ash or clay into an intricate form of writing. The geometric drawings carry messages, stories and knowledge among roughly 80 ethnolinguistic groups.

The Baltic song and dance celebrations can assemble as many as 40,000 singers and dancers at once. Most are amateurs who rehearse for years before the enormous festivals held every four or five years.
locationContext: Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania · Baltic region, Northern Europe

fact: Aka communities developed complex four-part contrapuntal singing without written notation. Singers improvise and alter their voices during a piece, making the music seem to change continuously, while children learn by joining rituals from an early age.
locationContext: South-western Central African Republic · Central Africa

country: Saudi Arabia, Oman and United Arab Emirates
fact: Camel herders use a sung oral tradition called Alheda'a to direct their animals. Camels are trained to distinguish calls for right and left, open their mouths on request, kneel to be ridden and assemble quickly during danger.
locationContext: Arabian Peninsula · Saudi Arabia, Oman and United Arab Emirates

fact: Falconry is practised by people of all ages in more than eighty countries. Skills are passed on through mentoring, within families and through clubs and schools, keeping a longstanding human partnership with birds alive.
On La Gomera, islanders can reproduce spoken Castilian Spanish as whistles, turning ordinary language into signals that carry across the island’s deep ravines.

In Catalonia, teams called colles build human towers several levels high in public squares. Hundreds of people can form the base, while a child climbs to the top and raises a hand to complete the castell.

photoCredit: U.S. National Park Service · public domain
fact: Garifuna songs and dances carry history and traditional knowledge across generations. Their living tradition blends African and Indigenous Caribbean influences and is shared by communities across four Central American countries.
locationContext: Caribbean coast · Belize, Guatemala, Honduras and Nicaragua

fact: An angklung is made from tuned bamboo tubes that sound when shaken. Because one instrument usually contributes only a note or chord, a complete melody depends on a whole group listening and playing together.
Kutiyattam is one of India's oldest living theatrical traditions. Performers use an intricate language of eye movements, facial expressions and hand gestures to unfold Sanskrit drama for an audience.
The enormous Epic of King Gesar survives not just as text but through singers and storytellers who perform its episodes. The tradition also feeds Tibetan opera, painting and other community arts.
locationContext: Tibetan Plateau and Inner Mongolia · China

place: Wine Horses of Caravaca de la Cruz
fact: Each May in Caravaca de la Cruz, horses wear spectacular cloaks embroidered with silk and gold thread. Four handlers then run beside each horse in a race up the steep approach to the castle.
locationContext: Caravaca de la Cruz, Murcia · south-eastern Spain

country: Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and United Arab Emirates
fact: Serving Arabic coffee is a carefully learned language of hospitality. The host prepares it for guests, serves the eldest or most important person first and pours small amounts so cups can be offered repeatedly.
locationContext: Arabian Peninsula · Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and United Arab Emirates

fact: Tibetan opera combines folk song, dance, storytelling, chanting and brightly painted masks in one performance tradition. Stories pass between generations while also teaching history and social values.

Deepavali brings families and communities together to light lamps, exchange gifts and sweets, share meals and celebrate with music, dance and rituals. The practices vary widely while the light remains a shared symbol of hope and renewal.
locationContext: India · South Asia and communities worldwide

fact: On Peru's Taquile Island, textile making is shared across the community: men traditionally knit while women spin wool and weave. Clothing is both practical and a visible record of social life and identity.
locationContext: Taquile Island, Lake Titicaca · southern Peru

fact: On Kihnu and Manija, women became the principal custodians of an island culture of runic songs, games, dances, wedding ceremonies and handicrafts while many men worked at sea.
locationContext: Kihnu and Manija islands · Gulf of Riga, Estonia

place: Bistritsa Babi of the Shoplouk region
fact: In Bistritsa, elderly women preserve an archaic form of Shoplouk polyphony alongside ring dances and seasonal rituals, passing the repertoire between generations.

place: Ritual dance of the royal drum
fact: Burundi's royal-drum tradition is not drumming alone: synchronized rhythms unfold with dancers, heroic poetry and traditional songs, turning the drum into a complete community performance.

place: Saman dance of the Gayo people
fact: Saman dancers perform in tight seated rows, creating rapid shared rhythms by clapping, striking their chests and thighs, tapping the ground and clicking their fingers while singing verses.
locationContext: Gayo communities · Aceh province, Sumatra, Indonesia

fact: Bauls are mystic minstrels who travel from village to village, singing a spiritual philosophy with simple instruments including the one-string ektara. Their song language keeps evolving to stay meaningful to new listeners.
locationContext: Rural Bangladesh · Bengal region, South Asia

fact: The Makishi masquerade appears at the end of mukanda, an annual initiation for boys aged roughly eight to twelve. Masked characters return to the community to celebrate and teach through dance and performance.
locationContext: North-western and western Zambia · southern Africa

fact: Across Mongolia each July, Naadam brings communities together for three traditional games: long-distance horse racing, wrestling and archery. Music, clothing, crafts and ritual surround the competitions.
At Oostduinkerke, fishers ride strong Brabant horses breast-deep into the North Sea. Each horse pulls a funnel-shaped net that sieves shrimp from the sand as the pair walks parallel to shore.
An official count on 28 August 2026 recorded just 222 Tristan da Cunha islanders. The entire resident community is centred on one settlement, Edinburgh of the Seven Seas.
locationContext: Edinburgh of the Seven Seas · Tristan da Cunha, South Atlantic

fact: Sultan Kösen was first confirmed as the world's tallest living man in 2009 at 246.5 centimetres. Guinness also measured his hands at 28.5 centimetres from wrist to middle fingertip.
Jyoti Amge was measured at 62.8 centimetres tall in Nagpur on her eighteenth birthday, 16 December 2011, earning the Guinness title of shortest woman living.
The fujara is a Slovak shepherds' flute that can stand up to two metres long yet has only three finger holes. Players shape its deep, meditative music through breath and harmonic overtones.
Japanese washi is made by hand from paper-mulberry fibres through skills shared across whole communities. The craft produces remarkably strong paper despite its light, translucent appearance.

At Kyoto's Gion Matsuri, a local boy serves as a sacred messenger whose feet do not touch the ground from 13 July until the first parade ends. The largest hoko floats can reach 25 metres and weigh 12 tonnes.
The Royal Ballet of Cambodia uses codified hand gestures, controlled movement and elaborate costumes to enact legends. Its dancers were closely associated with the Khmer royal court for centuries.
Cremona's master luthiers hand-carve each violin from spruce and maple without prefabricated components, assembling over seventy distinct pieces in a tradition dating to 1539.
Capoeira players take turns sparring with flowing acrobatic kicks inside a singing circle, matching their tempo directly to the commanding rhythm of the berimbau bow.

photoCredit: InSapphoWeTrust from Los Angeles, Califo · CC BY-SA 2.0
fact: Mariachi ensembles bring together violins, trumpets, and the round-backed guitarrón bass to perform regional songs rooted in western Mexican rural gatherings.
Flamenco fuses passionate cante vocals, percussive guitar and dynamic footwork, expressing grief, longing, and joy across Andalusia's communities.
Born in the working-class ports of Buenos Aires and Montevideo, tango combines intimate partner dancing with the soulful, melancholic sound of the bandoneón accordion.
Gagaku has been performed in Japan's imperial court for more than a millennium, blending wind instruments like the sho mouth organ with ancient dance and precise ritual.
Al-Ayyala performers form two facing rows of men holding slender bamboo wands, moving together in rhythm with booming drums and chanted poetry celebrating bravery.
locationContext: Abu Dhabi and Al Ain · United Arab Emirates

photoCredit: Rollan Budi from Kuta, Bali,, Indonesia · CC BY-SA 2.0
fact: Kecak features a seated circle of up to one hundred men chanting continuous 'cak-cak' vocal rhythms, depicting epic Ramayana battles without any instrumental accompaniment.
A single master puppeteer, the dalang, manipulates intricate water-buffalo leather puppets behind a backlit screen for hours while singing and directing a full gamelan orchestra.
Noh drama uses carved wooden masks, stylised gliding footsteps, and poetic chanting to evoke supernatural tales on a minimalist cypress-wood stage.
The two-stringed wooden dombra is played solo to perform kuys—narrative musical poems that evoke historical legends, philosophical reflections, and steppe galloping.

place: Craftsmanship and performance art of the Tar
fact: The tar is an eleven-stringed, figure-of-eight lute carved from mulberry wood and covered in cattle heart-membrane, serving as the central lead instrument of Azerbaijani mugham.
locationContext: Baku and Shusha · Azerbaijan, South Caucasus

photoCredit: 단원 김홍도 (檀園 金弘道, 1745 - 1816 이후) · Public domain
fact: In Korean ssireum wrestling, two competitors grab a fabric belt called a satba tied around their opponent's waist and thigh, using technique and balance to topple the other without striking.

photoCredit: Pedro Ribeiro Simões from Lisboa, Portug · CC BY 2.0
fact: Fado blends poetic verses of longing and fate with the delicate twelve-string Portuguese guitar, originating in nineteenth-century maritime taverns of Lisbon.

photoCredit: Kevon Rhiney and Romain Cruse · CC BY 4.0
fact: Originating in Kingston in the late 1960s, reggae emerged as a voice for social justice, human rights, and spirituality, distinguished by its offbeat accents and heavy basslines.
Venice's Regata Storica has taken place along the Grand Canal since the thirteenth century, with costumed rowers propelling historic galleys standing up facing forward.
locationContext: Grand Canal, Venice · Veneto, north-eastern Italy

fact: Bertsolaris compose and sing rhymed, metred verses entirely on the spot in the ancient Basque language, debating philosophical and everyday prompts before thousands of spectators.
locationContext: Gipuzkoa and Biscay · Basque Country, northern Spain

fact: Frevo dancers in Recife sprint and jump through crowd-filled streets at breakneck speeds, executing acrobatic steps while balancing small, colourful open umbrellas.
locationContext: Recife and Olinda, Pernambuco · north-eastern Brazil

fact: Georgian polyphony is an ancient secular and sacred singing tradition featuring complex three-part vocal harmonies and unique scales that predated Western European notation.
With over three million saunas for 5.5 million inhabitants, the Finnish sauna is an essential communal ritual of cleansing, tranquility, and bonding practiced across all generations.
locationContext: Helsinki and Tampere · Finland, Northern Europe

fact: The art of the Neapolitan pizzaiuolo involves a four-stage process including the spinning rotatorio movement of the dough and rapid baking in a wood-fired oven at nearly 485 degrees Celsius.
Sicilian puppet theatre features heavy hand-carved wooden marionettes dressed in hand-beaten nickel-silver armour, manipulated on iron rods to stage epic medieval chivalric battles.
locationContext: Palermo and Catania, Sicily · southern Italy

fact: Canto a tenore is an archaic Sardinian polyphonic singing style where deep guttural bass and baritone voices intentionally imitate the sounds of winds and bleating livestock.
During the Varia di Palmi festival, two hundred volunteer bearers carry a 16-metre wooden sacred machine weighing twenty tonnes through crowded streets on their bare shoulders.
Farmers on the windswept volcanic island of Pantelleria dig deep stone hollows to plant head-trained dwarf vines below ground level, harvesting sweet Zibibbo grapes by hand in desert winds.
locationContext: Pantelleria Island, Strait of Sicily · southern Italy

fact: Venetian perlere melt thin coloured glass rods over hot torch flames to spin perforated beads that have served as coveted Mediterranean adornments and currency since the 14th century.
locationContext: Murano and Venice, Veneto · north-eastern Italy

fact: Italian truffle hunters rely on oral lore and keen scent-trained dogs to harvest elusive subterranean truffles, carefully replacing topsoil to preserve delicate fungal mycelium webs.
The traditional French gastronomic meal follows a strict sequence of courses celebrating terroir, precise wine pairings, and the ritual table arts of tasting and conversation.

photoCredit: Musée des Beaux-arts et de la Dentelle d'Alençon · Public Domain
fact: Crafting one square centimetre of Alençon needle lace requires up to seven hours of microscopic hand stitching using pure linen thread and an array of delicate horsehair outlines.
At Breton Fest-Noz night gatherings, hundreds of dancers link their little fingers in continuous serpent chains, locking footwork to the call-and-response rhythm of the bombarde and biniou pipes.

place: Perfume skills of Pays de Grasse
fact: In the sheltered valley of Grasse, perfumers harvest Centifolia roses at dawn to preserve volatile morning oils, distilling centuries of fragrance heritage into world-famous essences.
locationContext: Pays de Grasse, Côte d'Azur · south-eastern France

fact: Artisanal zinc roofers hand-cut, fold, and solder interlocking blue-grey zinc sheets across seventy percent of Paris, maintaining the historic roofscape designed during Haussmann's 19th-century rebuild.
Performed every August since the mid-15th century inside the Basilica of Santa Maria, the Mystery Play of Elche lowers choral actors from the dome inside a gilded mechanical pomegranate sphere.

During the medieval festival of La Patum, dancing giants, fire-breathing dragons, and masked figures packed into Berga's town square dance through whirlwinds of exploding sparks to pounding tabal drums.

place: Fiesta of the Patios in Córdoba
fact: Every spring, residents of Córdoba open their private whitewashed courtyards to visitors, displaying hundreds of hanging potted geraniums, jasmine, and orange trees tended year-round for communal beauty.

Neighbourhood artists across Valencia spend months building multi-storey satirical wooden sculptures, erecting nearly 800 monuments across the city before setting them all ablaze at midnight on St Joseph's Day.
During Holy Week in Hellín and Calanda, up to twenty thousand drummers in flowing black tunics gather in town centres to play relentless unison percussion that echoes across the valleys for days.
German organ builders individually shape and voice thousands of lead-tin pipes by hand, tuning air resonance to the exact architectural acoustics of ancient stone cathedrals.
On Shrove Tuesday in Binche, up to a thousand Gilles don wax masks and metre-tall ostrich feather headdresses to parade through town, tossing blood oranges to crowds as symbols of prosperity.

place: Procession of the Holy Blood in Bruges
fact: Over eighteen hundred local citizens dress in medieval and renaissance costumes every Ascension Day to walk through the cobbled canals of Bruges, carrying historical reliquaries.
At the summit of Oudenberg hill, town officials toss ten thousand round bread rolls known as krakelingen into celebrating crowds before lighting a colossal bonfire to chase away winter.
Dating back to 1411, jousters in Namur mount two-metre wooden stilts and use elbows, shoulders, and foot parries in square arenas to knock opposing teams to the cobblestones.

place: Indigenous festivity dedicated to the dead
fact: Indigenous communities lay bright orange cempasúchil marigold petals and copal incense trails from doorways to cemeteries, guiding the wandering souls of ancestors back for night-long feasts.
Charros and escaramuzas demonstrate high-speed lasso tricks and side-saddle riding dressed in wide-brimmed sombreros and silver-studded suits, accompanied by live brass ensembles.

place: Parachicos in the Great Feast of Chiapa de Corzo
fact: Thousands of dancers in carved cedar masks and ixtle wigs shake tin chinchín rattles to honour Saint Sebastian, dancing non-stop across Chiapa de Corzo for six consecutive days.
locationContext: Chiapa de Corzo, Chiapas · southern Mexico

place: La Romería of the Virgin of Zapopan
fact: Over two million pilgrims walk nine kilometres alongside twenty-five thousand indigenous feather-crested dancers, escorting a small 16th-century wooden image from Guadalajara to Zapopan.
locationContext: Guadalajara and Zapopan, Jalisco · western Mexico

fact: Four Quechua communities gather every June to weave thousands of metres of q'oya grass into thick cables, entirely rebuilding a twenty-eight-metre Inca suspension bridge in three days.

place: Festivity of Virgen de la Candelaria of Puno
fact: Forty thousand Quechua and Aymara dancers in horned devil masks dance along the shores of Lake Titicaca, accompanied by three hundred brass marching bands playing in thin Andean air.

place: Pilgrimage of the Lord of Qoyllurit'i
fact: Up to ninety thousand pilgrims trek to an isolated glacier valley at 4,700 metres elevation, where masked Ukuku dancers stand vigil at sub-zero temperatures beneath snow-covered peaks.
locationContext: Sinakara Valley, Cusco · southern Peruvian Andes

fact: Peruvian artisanal fishermen harvest fresh Pacific catch that is cured within minutes using sour Piuran limes, rocoto peppers, and red onions, preserving a culinary craft dating back to the Moche civilisation.
locationContext: Lima and Piura · Pacific coast of Peru

fact: Held only once every four years in the Tyrolean Alps, the Schemenlaufen features paired dancers in hand-carved masks carrying iron bells weighing up to thirty-five kilograms to welcome spring.
Master artisans apply protective gum using hand-carved pearwood blocks before submerging linen into deep indigo vats, creating white geometric patterns against brilliant dark blue cloth.
Staged only once every twenty to twenty-five years since 1797 on Lake Geneva, the Winegrowers' Festival brings together over five thousand performers to honour vineyard workers.

At precisely 4:00 AM on the Monday after Ash Wednesday, all streetlights in Basel are extinguished for the Morgestraich, when thousands of masked piccolo and drum cliques step into the darkness behind glowing hand-painted lanterns.

During Mendrisio's night processions, the town switches off its street lamps and is lit solely by trasparenti: luminous translucent paintings stretched over wooden frames glowing like stained glass in the dark.

Craftsmen in Nusnäs carve iconic Dala horses by hand from slow-growth siljan pine, decorating each statuette with two-colour kurbits floral brushstrokes first developed during long winter nights in the 18th century.
On the longest day of the year, Swedish communities weave crowns of fresh wildflowers and raise birch-leaf-covered majstång poles, singing ring-dances under near-constant daylight.
In classical Bunraku theatre, each large puppet is operated in synchronized coordination by three visible master puppeteers, moving eyebrows, fingers, and eyes in tandem with a chanting narrator.
During Tokushima's Awa Odori festival, over one hundred thousand dancers wearing crescent-shaped woven rush hats parading through lantern-lit boulevards to syncopated shamisen and taiko beats.
The Kumbh Mela brings tens of millions of pilgrims to bathe at the sacred confluence of the Ganges and Yamuna rivers, making it the largest peaceful gathering of humanity recorded on Earth.

place: Kalbelia folk songs and dances of Rajasthan
fact: Kalbelia dancers wear flowing black skirts embroidered with mirror-work, performing acrobatic backbends and spinning turns designed to mimic the sinuous movements of desert cobras.
The Carnival of Barranquilla merges Indigenous, African, and European carnival traditions, highlighted by the irreverent Marimonda character with its long floppy trunk and mismatched ears.
Recorded in ancient Celtic myth and brehon law for three millennia, hurling is played with carved ash hurleys striking a leather ball at speeds exceeding 150 kilometres per hour.
Unlike mouth-blown bagpipes, Irish uilleann pipes are powered entirely by an elbow-driven bellows, allowing the seated player to accompany complex melodies with keyed harmonic regulators.
locationContext: County Clare and Dublin · western Ireland

fact: In the Scottish caber toss, athletes hoist a five-metre tapered trunk of Scottish larch weighing up to eighty kilograms, launching it end-over-end to land directly in a 12 o'clock position.

Norway's national instrument, the Hardanger fiddle, features four bowed melody strings and up to five sympathetic understrings that vibrate freely beneath the fingerboard, creating an ethereal ringing resonance.
Often called the Greek blues, Rebetiko emerged in port taverns after 1922, weaving sorrowful lyrics of displacement with the distinctive metallic timbre of the long-necked bouzouki.
Sung without any instruments by amateur choral groups in rural taverns, Canto Alentejano pairs a solo lead voice with a deep unison choir echoing across the sunbaked plains of southern Portugal.
locationContext: Serpa and Beja, Alentejo · southern Portugal

fact: A skilled Khöömei throat singer manipulates their throat muscles to generate two distinct pitches at the exact same moment: a deep gravelly drone and a high-pitched whistling flute melody.

Master craftsmen carve translucent figures from cured donkey hide, painting them in mineral dyes and articulating joints with wire rods so puppeteers can create moving silhouettes behind paper screens.

photoCredit: Moroccan Ministry of Culture · CC BY-SA 4.0
fact: In the Tbourida equestrian exhibition, a troop of horsemen in embroidered silk jellabas gallop abreast at breakneck speed, firing their antique black-powder muskets in a single explosive collective blast.
locationContext: Meknes and El Jadida · central Morocco

fact: Depicted on 4,000-year-old tomb reliefs in Minya, Tahteeb is a non-violent stick martial art where duelists swirl heavy rattan staves in time to folk pipe and drum beats.
locationContext: Luxor and Qena, Upper Egypt · Nile River Valley

fact: The Armenian duduk is carved exclusively from seasoned wild apricot wood, using an oversized cane reed that produces a haunting, mournful sound often compared to the human voice.
locationContext: Yerevan and Garni · southern Caucasus, Armenia

fact: In Dalmatian stone alleys, klapa circles sing unconducted four-part harmonies without any instruments, blending natural tenors and deep basses to celebrate maritime life and love.
locationContext: Split and Dubrovnik, Dalmatia · Adriatic Croatia

fact: Over twenty-eight thousand masked dancers and ten thousand musicians parade continuously for twenty hours across the high Altiplano, enacting the eternal battle between archangels and subterranean mining devils.

place: Traditional weaving of the Ecuadorian toquilla straw hat
photoCredit: Agencia de Noticias ANDES · CC BY-SA 2.0
fact: The authentic Panama hat originates solely in Ecuador, where weavers split wild Carludovica palm straw into fibres so fine that an exquisite hat requires up to six months of weaving and can hold water.
locationContext: Montecristi and Cuenca · coastal and Andean Ecuador

fact: Javanese and Balinese gamelan orchestras consist of up to forty hand-forged bronze metallophones and tuned gongs, played communally without a written score or individual conductor.

photoCredit: Korea.net / Korean Culture and Information Service · CC BY-SA 2.0
fact: In late autumn, extended families and neighbours across South Korea gather for Kimjang, washing and fermenting hundreds of heads of cabbage in communal earthenware onggi jars to share for the winter.

place: Washoku, traditional dietary cultures of the Japanese
fact: Washoku culinary philosophy balances five natural colours and five distinct cooking techniques, using kelp and bonito dashi broths to elevate the natural seasonal flavours of ingredients.
In rural Cuba, campesino poets spar in witty musical duels known as Punto, improvising rhymed ten-line décima stanzas on the spot to the strum of the Spanish guitar and laud.
locationContext: Pinar del Río and Sancti Spíritus · western Cuba

place: Mola textile art of the Guna people
fact: Guna indigenous women stitch intricate molas by layering up to seven contrasting coloured cotton cloths, cutting away patterns with razors to reveal hidden mythical and natural designs.
locationContext: Guna Yala archipelago · Caribbean coast of Panama

fact: Preserved in Maya Achí language without written alteration since the 15th century, Rabinal Achí dramatizes ancient highland political conflict with carved masks and low wooden trumpets.

place: Winter festivities of the Caretos of Podence
fact: Young men disguised in suits made of red, green, and yellow fringed wool wear pointed tin masks and rattle leather belts of cowbells as they dart wildly through village cobblestone streets.
locationContext: Podence, Macedo de Cavaleiros · north-eastern Portugal

fact: In the Ostrobothnian village of Kaustinen, a community of hundreds of amateur violinists learns intricate, syncopated 18th-century wedding polskas purely by ear without formal sheet music.
In southern Estonia, chimneyless log smoke saunas are heated for half a day with birch logs until stones are white-hot, creating an aromatic smoky heat used for bodily and spiritual cleansing.
Sutartinės songs are performed by small female ensembles singing strict polyphonic canons built upon acoustic dissonances of major seconds, walking in interlocking rhythmic circles as they sing.
The Polonaise is a stately processional dance in triple metre led by the first couple, in which hundreds of dancers weave sweeping geometric figures through historic ballrooms and plazas.

place: Ancient Georgian traditional Qvevri wine-making method
fact: Dating back eight thousand years, Georgian vintners ferment whole crushed grapes with skins, stalks, and pips inside massive egg-shaped clay qvevri vessels buried completely underground for natural temperature control.
Makonde sculptors carve single trunks of dense African blackwood into towering Dimoongo trees of life, sculpting dozens of climbing interconnected human figures that support one another.

place: Mbira music of the Shona people
fact: The mbira dzavadzimu features twenty-two hand-forged metal keys mounted on a hardwood soundboard and placed inside a dried calabash gourd, producing polyrhythmic cycles to invite ancestral communication.

place: Isukuti dance of Isukha and Idakho communities
photoCredit: UNESCO / Western Kenya Cultural Team · CC BY-SA 3.0
fact: The energetic Isukuti dance is driven by three distinct barrel drums (mutanda, tsikhati, and ifuchere) and an antelope horn, keeping dancers moving in rapid, undulating torso shakes.
Weavers in Bonwire operate narrow horizontal strip-looms with both hands and feet, interlacing silk and cotton threads into geometric patterns where every individual colour symbolises royal proverbs.

place: Ceebu Jën, a culinary art of Senegal
fact: Ceebu Jën is an elaborate one-pot national dish created in the coastal city of Saint-Louis, where fresh white fish is stuffed with aromatic herbs and simmered in broken rice with cassava, pumpkin, and tamarind.

place: Ritual and ceremonies of Sebiba in Djanet
fact: In the Sahara oasis of Djanet, Tuareg male dancers in indigo robes and silver swords dance ritual duels on sand dunes while female drummers sing hypnotic rhythms on ganga tambours.
locationContext: Djanet Oasis, Tassili n'Ajjer · southern Algeria

place: Pottery skills of the women of Sejnane
fact: Berber women in Sejnane fashion terra cotta vessels without potters' wheels, burnishing raw clay with polished sea shells and firing them in open brush hearths before painting with lentisk sap.

place: Al-Khanjar, craft skills and social practices
fact: The curved silver Omani khanjar dagger is handcrafted through delicate filigree and granulation work, worn around the waist on woven camel-hair belts as a national symbol of status and male maturity.
locationContext: Muscat and Nizwa · Sultanate of Oman

place: Traditional craft skills and arts of Al-Mudhif
photoCredit: US Army / Staff Sgt. Michel Sauret · Public Domain
fact: In the Mesopotamian Marshes, Marsh Arabs construct towering cathedral-like communal guest houses called mudhifs entirely out of bundled giant reeds, erecting parabolic arches without a single nail or wooden post.

The Radif is a classical repertoire of over two hundred modal melodic motifs memorized by master lutenists, forming the foundation for meditative, virtuosic improvisation on the long-necked tar and setar.

photoCredit: Uzbek Ministry of Culture · CC BY-SA 4.0
fact: Dating back to the Silk Road oasis of Khiva, the Lazgi dance begins with slow, frozen postures before exploding into rapid shivering finger movements and acrobatic spins representing the reawakening of nature.

place: Khon, masked dance drama in Thailand
fact: Khon dancers train for years in royal academies to master specialized body languages without speaking, wearing lacquered paper-mâché masks encrusted with gold leaf and glass mirrors while a piphat orchestra plays.

place: Quan Họ Bắc Ninh folk songs
fact: In villages of the Red River Delta, pairs of female singers wearing flat palm-leaf quai thao hats trade improvised poetic verses across waterways with male partners, singing complex melodic ornaments without instrumental accompaniment.
locationContext: Bắc Ninh and Bắc Giang, Red River Delta · northern Vietnam

fact: During rice harvest season on ancient two-thousand-year-old mountain terraces, elder Ifugao women chant the Hudhud epic for days on end, reciting centuries of customary law and heroic lore in intricate metred verses.

In north-east Arnhem Land, Yolŋu custodians craft the sacred yidaki from living eucalyptus trunks hollowed out by termites, playing complex circular-breathing rhythms that imitate kookaburras, dingoes, and thunder.
